When we go back to Kalamazoo, [unintelligible] Johnson, he’ll be there, and he knows where the plane’s going to land, it don’t land at O’Hare main field, it places outside, you know, he’d be right there with his car to pick us up, bring us back to the plane, step from his car into the plane. He really takes care of us. And they say he’s starting this scholarship too. I don’t know what that will come to, not very much I don’t think [Hap laughs].

segments.speaker: Hap Moody
segments.words: Two pretty good players.

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.words: So they really cracked some ribs, huh?

segments.speaker: Hap Moody
segments.words: Yeah. It wasn’t too bad, just tried to breathe for a while. And I wouldn’t even know it. unintelligible autographed by Walker and Kramer and that bunch. They’d call me down on to the field, a bunch of ‘em. I came out unintelligible the football.

segments.speaker: Bertha Clyde Moody
segments.words: Yeah, and he’d tell them what they did that was wrong, and so this one time, he was showing them what they did that was wrong, and he did the same thing, and boy did they…

segments.speaker: Hap Moody
segments.words: Taking moving pictures of it, so they couldn’t get out of it Hap laughs.

segments.speaker: Bertha Clyde Moody
segments.words: But when he feels good, and they practice, sometimes they practice twice a day, in spring football practice…

segments.speaker: Hap Moody
segments.words: in April.

segments.speaker: Bertha Clyde Moody
segments.words: And he would walk up there and come home and go back for the afternoon practice, and nearly always got a ride back with somebody, but he always walked up.

segments.speaker: Hap Moody
segments.words: Bob Haynes, he drives right by the house, he’s professor there at the [unintelligible] plant, engineering plant, down in the unintelligible there. So he always comes over to see if I’ve got a ride. I never have to walk home.

segments.speaker: Bertha Clyde Moody
segments.words: But last spring he missed it all.

segments.speaker: Hap Moody
segments.words: Yeah, last spring I was in the unintelligible hospital for three weeks. Sam: And the team didn’t do too well last year, did they?

segments.speaker: Bertha Clyde Moody
segments.words: Oh Bertha laughs. Let’s not lay that on Hap. Bertha laughs cut Sam: What was it like working for Dr. Robinson?

segments.speaker: Bertha Clyde Moody
segments.words: Well, I just typed names on the envelopes and help put out the mail, I didn’t work at the place that they put out the lessons. I mean where they worked them up. But we used to have lots of fun.

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.words: Did you know Dr. Robinson? Did you…

segments.speaker: Bertha Clyde Moody
segments.words: Yeah, yeah. Hap was a real good friend of Dr. Robinson.

segments.speaker: Hap Moody
segments.words: Yeah, I had a special deputy. He gave me a gold badge for making him the special deputy. Sam: What was he like? How do you remember him?

segments.speaker: Hap Moody
segments.words: Well I first knew him as just an ordinary clerk in the corner drugstore. He wasn’t anything but just an ordinary clerk in the corner drugstore. And I don’t know just how they got started on this stuff. Hap laughs Oh yeah.

segments.speaker: Bertha Clyde Moody
segments.words: Actually, he was, he did lots of good, he didn’t want his name announced, kids would be lost…

segments.speaker: Hap Moody
segments.words: He’d hire an airplane to search for ‘em.

segments.speaker: Bertha Clyde Moody
segments.words: Yeah, but he didn’t want his name…

segments.speaker: Hap Moody
segments.words: …his name in it all. He always drank his coffee out of a saucer Hap laughs. Yeah, he was pretty generous Hap laughs. Let’s see…

segments.speaker: Bertha Clyde Moody
segments.words: The year that…

segments.speaker: Hap Moody
segments.words: unintelligible on one of these raids, I guess, and that was…

segments.speaker: Bertha Clyde Moody
segments.words: No, are you gonna tell him about her getting, loaning the money. After Charlie Summerfield died, Hap and I went huckleberrying. And we would go out and pick huckleberries for three or four days, come back, and sell them for a dollar a gallon. And…

segments.speaker: Hap Moody
segments.words: We picked 285 gallons.

segments.speaker: Bertha Clyde Moody
segments.words: 287 gallons. [Sam whistles]. And the paper said that “assisted by Mrs. Moody” always. That burned me up Bertha laughs. Well, anyway, Hap run for office that fall, and we came in from huckleberrying, and course Hap had gotten his sleeve torn and had these old pants on, and so on. And we went down to the Idaho Inn for, it wasn’t called Idaho Inn then, I guess, but anyway, the paper, they put up all the returns. And Hap had a big safety pin, as I recall, in his sleeve, and Doc said something about it, and Hap stuck out his hand, like he needed some money, and Doc went home and told the missus, and you know she called up the next day. And she wanted to know if Hap really needed money. Hap laughs But we huckleberried, we began at Beales Butte, I guess, and just went clear round, and we picked a few huckleberries on Mount Hood.

segments.speaker: Hap Moody
segments.words: Down in Oregon. You see, [unintelligible] in July, and Democrats put in a man of the name of Berry as sheriff. And [Hap laugh]s so we picked huckleberries and campaigned against Mr. Berry.[ Hap laughs] Guess they should have been smarter than that because at the end of the day they’d have had a Democrat sheriff for six months. Sam: Why, you did, say they should have been smarter. Is that because he didn’t stand much of a chance against you?

segments.speaker: Hap Moody
segments.words: Well, they should have known that the chief deputy should have been appointed for the rest of that term, you know, six months.

segments.speaker: Bertha Clyde Moody
segments.words: Where the sheriff was a Republican, this is generally what happens, but anyway. Sam: Did Dr. Robinson have a lot of influence in Moscow itself? I’d understood that the religion, that his religion, Psychiana, was kept out of the area.

segments.speaker: Hap Moody
segments.words: Never, never, he never…

segments.speaker: Bertha Clyde Moody
segments.words: That’s right, we couldn’t...

segments.speaker: Hap Moody
segments.words: Never put a letter out in Moscow. Never. Always foreign countries.

segments.speaker: Bertha Clyde Moody
segments.words: If they was an address, he bought addresses, and if there was an address to anybody here in Moscow, we threw it out. Sam: What was the reason for that? Do you know?

segments.speaker: Bertha Clyde Moody
segments.words: I haven’t any idea.

segments.speaker: Hap Moody
segments.words: No. He worked god-forbidden foreign lands, because I know he got several thousand dollars from some unintelligible faith over in India. Yeah, he had the visions you know, he talked to the…

segments.speaker: Bertha Clyde Moody
segments.words: He talked to mother, wasn’t it his mother, uncle, somebody. But anyway, now one of the things that was in his book was: goldfish jumped out of the goldfish bowl. And he was going to put it back in, he thought well if it could jump out, it could jump back in.

segments.speaker: Hap Moody
segments.words: And it did. [Hap laughs]

segments.speaker: Bertha Clyde Moody
segments.words: You know, this is something I don’t know whether anybody that worked for him really knew and understood about. Course all I did was, as I say, I typed addresses, and we stuffed, we’d get tired, she’d let us change, and we’d stuff envelopes with these lessons. Sam: Did he seem like a religious person in the same way that the reverends and you know the heads of the churches around did?

segments.speaker: Hap Moody
segments.words: No, not exactly. He got to be a bishop, you know.

segments.speaker: Bertha Clyde Moody
segments.words: Well, that was his title, yeah. I really couldn’t, I don’t know. Sam: I just wondered how he seemed, that’s all.

segments.speaker: Bertha Clyde Moody
segments.words: Uh huh. He was big guy. I remember one time we was in Portland. He had this huge diamond ring, and we couldn’t see him when we went in this hotel, we couldn’t see him, but the way he was sitting we could see that diamond ring, and Hap said that has to be Doc Robinson. And it was! We liked him. We wasn’t that close, you know, that we knew that much about him. Sam: I think few people did, really.

segments.speaker: Bertha Clyde Moody
segments.words: Yeah, I think that’s true. Yeah.

segments.speaker: Hap Moody
segments.words: He was generous. He gave away lots of money.

segments.speaker: Bertha Clyde Moody
segments.words: But I guess Alfred didn’t want anything to do with it. And I don’t know whether they have anything left or not, you know, of his lessons and stuff.

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.words: I think there’s some records at the university, in the library.

segments.speaker: Bertha Clyde Moody
segments.words: I hope, I really do. But people would come. One of the girls that lived upstairs, her mother would write and ask about this Psychiana, you know. Well, we didn’t know enough to tell her anything. He had those two buildings that he had workers in. And the first day that I worked Bertha laughs he had a heart attack and they had to take him on the stretcher and Hap said that was some scenery work. Hap laughs Jenny Nesbitt was at the head of the building where I worked, and that was down in the professional building. And then the other was up here. We called it “Sam’s.”

segments.speaker: Hap Moody
segments.words: Used to be Sam’s Furniture. It’s now Dahman, now, I guess, insurance. Weisel, Weisel’s insurance building now.

segments.speaker: Bertha Clyde Moody
segments.words: But I tell you, some of us ladies had a good time. Doc would come in and we’d quiet down [Bertha laughs]. It got to be, we had I think ten minutes that we could go out, either morning or afternoon, for, get a cup of coffee or whatever we wanted to do. And you know, it gets to be, fifteen, twenty, half an hour, and he watched, I guess, some of us, and so he put a stop to our staying so long. But that’s all right, anybody else would too. [pause] His daughter and Alf was going to school. And I liked those kids too, but we knew ‘em. Hap knew Doc better than I did.

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.words: Names of streets and…

segments.speaker: Bertha Clyde Moody
segments.words: …everything. Let’s see. It started out with Pine. Larch. Cedar.

segments.speaker: Hap Moody
segments.words: Oak. “Owns.”

segments.speaker: Bertha Clyde Moody
segments.words: “Potlatch Lumber Company Owns.” At that was Oak. “Everything” Elm. Maple was “Most.”

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.words: So put together it’s…

segments.speaker: Bertha Clyde Moody
segments.words: “Potlatch Lumber Company Owns.” Oh yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.words: “Owns Most Everything.”

segments.speaker: Bertha Clyde Moody
segments.words: “Everything Most,” because Maple was last.

segments.speaker: Hap Moody
segments.words: Going on up the hill.

segments.speaker: Bertha Clyde Moody
segments.words: They got some new ones I guess. At one time there was a Fir Street, that was used, temporary buildings down there. So I suppose that was "For Potlatch." Yep.

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.words: You said 66 prisoners at one time in the jail? in that little hole in the ground underneath the…this was later?

segments.speaker: Hap Moody
segments.words: No, no.

segments.speaker: Bertha Clyde Moody
segments.words: The one they tore down, to build this new one.

segments.speaker: Hap Moody
segments.words: They built the new jail in 1928. And it was a pretty good-sized jail, and it was course new, and that’s one reason that the federals, qualified to hold federal prisoners.

segments.speaker: Bertha Clyde Moody
segments.words: And that’s the one where they’d board on [unintelligible].

segments.speaker: Hap Moody
segments.words: There was a hole in the roof.

segments.speaker: Bertha Clyde Moody
segments.words: But things was, they wouldn’t be allowed to keep prisoners now like they did. Then you could put them together.

segments.speaker: Hap Moody
segments.words: They fed them twice a day, I guess now they have to feed ‘em three times.

segments.speaker: Bertha Clyde Moody
segments.words: But you did take in a lunch if they wanted it?

segments.speaker: Hap Moody
segments.words: Hm?

segments.speaker: Bertha Clyde Moody
segments.words: You did give ‘em a lunch though, I mean, and sandwich or something if they wanted it later, didn’t you? Sam: How many would you get in a cell, then?

segments.speaker: Hap Moody
segments.words: Hm?

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.words: How many would you put in a cell?

segments.speaker: Hap Moody
segments.words: Well you see the upstairs, there was two large rooms upstairs, and they had bunks, in big rooms. And there were smaller rooms when they’d get sick. And one room for crazy people. And then we could put them in the basement, that was a full basement under it, six or more down there, and then we had the kitchen and the dining room. unintelligible fill up the whole darn unintelligible if we had to Hap laughs. It was pretty crowded. And we always had a good cook, because all of them bootleggers, there was always a good cook amongst them. And of course, he did the cooking. And the dining room was next to the kitchen. And it wasn’t a very big kitchen, but it had a big stove.

segments.speaker: Bertha Clyde Moody
segments.words: And these old-fashioned electric stoves at the top heated. It would take about an hour to really heat up. But…

segments.speaker: Hap Moody
segments.words: He fed ‘em pancakes, [unintelligible] nine and four, twice a day.

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.words: How long would you keep them? Would you keep the federal prisoners for a pretty long time, too?

segments.speaker: Hap Moody
segments.words: Well, they say the average sentence in those days was eight months and a thousand dollar fine. Sam: And they stayed the entire…

segments.speaker: Hap Moody
segments.words: And they all got eight months and a thousand dollar fine. The fine [unintelligible] out the fines. Sam: Do you think that most of these guys resented being in jail a lot, or do you think a lot of them were pretty happy being there?

segments.speaker: Hap Moody
segments.words: Some of them were, I think.

segments.speaker: Bertha Clyde Moody
segments.words: Some of ‘em spent the winter there. It was a good place to spend their winter, I think. You know, if they couldn’t get work. It was a place to eat and sleep. Course, they was a lot of ‘em that wasn’t that way.

segments.speaker: Hap Moody
segments.words: I could swear that when I was up the road in Orofino in that county that they was waiting for them to come on by [Hap laughs] see ‘em by the way. Cause they must have known they was coming, lot of times.

segments.speaker: Bertha Clyde Moody
segments.words: They had these little electric stoves that they just wanted to heat up coffee or something real quick, too. But they didn’t have to wait the hour for the stove to heat up.

segments.speaker: Hap Moody
segments.words: In those days, were at the kangaroo court, a lot of them bootleggers had money, we had some of them had fourteen hundred dollars on ‘em. Put ‘em in jail. And we’d let them spend it. Helped us out a lot [Hap laughs].

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.words: you’d let them spend it on what?

segments.speaker: Hap Moody
segments.words: Oh, they’d spend on whatever they wanted to except drink. Tobacco. Sam: Did they have to pay for their own food, then, or just extra food?

segments.speaker: Bertha Clyde Moody
segments.words: It’d be extra.

segments.speaker: Hap Moody
segments.words: Extra, yeah.

segments.speaker: Bertha Clyde Moody
segments.words: It’d be extra, yeah, because they get the county unintelligible their regular eats. Sam: So how did that help them out, to be able to spend money?

segments.speaker: Bertha Clyde Moody
segments.words: It didn’t really help them out, only if they…

segments.speaker: Hap Moody
segments.words: That stuff was [unintelligible], in a way.

segments.speaker: Sam
segments.words: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Bertha Clyde Moody
segments.words: Maybe they was better satisfied. I don’t know. They could buy books or magazines. Sam: Do you think that most of the moonshiners came from the southern states, where they had a lot more of that going on?

segments.speaker: Hap Moody
segments.words: Lot of ‘em are care of Carolinas, Kentucky. Those was the two most of ‘em came from, Carolinas and Kentucky, that’s where most of them originated from. Sam: So they’d learned it back there, it was a part of their family background.

segments.speaker: Hap Moody
segments.words: Oh yeah. Yep. [long cut ambient noise and faint music]
